_meta.note: AI roster scouting reports keyed by team (players.team value). Generated by roster_reports.workflow.js from build_roster_inputs.py output. Sample seeded manually; run the workflow to fill the rest.

bench.helps: This is the best bench in the room — arguably better than the starters at several spots. Olsen (78 grade) averaged 16.7 ppg on 39.5% from three at South Alabama; King (39.3% from three, 47.7% overall) is an efficient combo guard; and Oboye (82 grade!) is a 7-1 rim-runner shooting 66.7% with 1.2 blocks. Freeman (79, 60.2 FG%, Creighton) gives a fourth quality big. Pearl can bring a 16-ppg scorer and a top-graded seven-footer off the pine — that's championship-level depth.
bench.hurts: The bench is where the shooting AND the usage problem both live, which is a deployment headache: Olsen is another high-volume scorer (16.7 ppg) who wants touches, and the drop-off is real at the very end — Walker (66 grade, 5 mpg, 52.9% on a tiny sample) and freshman Williams (70) aren't rotation-ready. The frontcourt is stacked (Ngoy/Oboye/Freeman/Dowd) but there's a logjam — only so many minutes for four quality bigs.

coach.might: Roll out the authored starting five — Pettiford and Kimble together in the backcourt, Overton on the wing, Dowd at the 4, freshman Ngoy at the 5 — and lean on the star grades and interior size, bringing Olsen and Oboye as the first scorers off the bench.
should: Fix the spacing math immediately: get Olsen (39.5%) and/or King (39.3%) into the closing lineup over one of the non-shooting guards. You cannot start Pettiford (29%) AND a non-shooting five and expect driving lanes — put at least three 39%+ shooters on the floor in crunch time or defenses will pack the paint.

Stagger Pettiford and Kimble rather than force the usage collision. Bring one off the bench to run a second unit as its lead scorer so each gets his own ball-dominant minutes; playing two sub-40% alphas together caps the efficiency of both.

Make Overton and Dowd the connective tissue. Overton (1.0 TO, 41.3%) and Dowd (2.1 apg from the 4) are your only reliable low-usage pieces — run the halfcourt through Dowd touches at the elbow so the guards play off the ball and Overton relocates for catch-and-shoot threes.

Weaponize the frontcourt depth on defense, not just for minutes. With Ngoy, Oboye (1.2 blk), Freeman (0.8 blk) and Dowd (1.3 blk) you can play drop-and-wall rim protection all 40 minutes and pressure the ball with Kimble (2.6 stl) — become a defense-and-size team that survives its poor perimeter shooting by winning the paint and the turnover battle.

Auburn.essence: A top-heavy, star-graded roster (five starters at 80-85, a bench that includes an 82 and a 79) built the modern way — a returning lead-guard headliner in Tahaad Pettiford surrounded by a full portal class of proven mid-major scorers and a five-star freshman five. The identity is size, interior defense, and scoring depth, not spacing: three legit shot-blocking bigs (Ngoy, Freeman, Oboye) and a double-double PF in Dowd anchor the paint, and the roster can throw 16-18 ppg scorers at you in waves. But the starting perimeter can't shoot — Pettiford (29% from three) and Kimble (34.8%) are the primary ball-handlers, and the two best shooters (Olsen 39.5%, King 39.3%) start on the bench. Steven Pearl inherits a loaded, deep, but spacing-challenged group with a real usage puzzle at guard.

second_unit.strength: Scoring and size that doesn't dip. A King-Olsen-Rubstavicius-Freeman-Oboye group can put a 16-ppg wing next to a 7-1 shot-blocker (Oboye, 82 grade) and a Creighton big (Freeman) — genuinely more shooting (King 39.3%, Olsen 39.5%) and rim protection than the actual starting five. The bench can win minutes outright, not just tread water.
second_unit.weakness: It's guard-light on creation and playmaking — King (1.6 apg) is the only real ball-handler, so the second unit can stagnate into hero-ball with Olsen hunting shots. And Rubstavicius is an unproven international freshman, so the wing defense and shot-making behind Overton is projection, not track record.

flaws.b: Only Overton (41.3%) clears 39% from three among the starters. Pettiford — the primary ball-handler — shot 29% from deep on 39.3% overall; Kimble is a middling 34.8%. Ngoy is an unproven freshman five with no shooting sample. Defenses will sag off Pettiford and wall the paint, and the two best shooters on the whole roster (Olsen 39.5%, King 39.3%) sit on the bench.
flaws.t: The starting perimeter can't space the floor

flaws.b: Kimble was THE scorer at EKU (18.0); Pettiford is the returning star (15.4). Both need the ball, and both shot under 40% from the field (Kimble 38.0%, Pettiford 39.3%). Playing them together is a usage collision between two sub-40% shooters — someone must accept off-ball reps neither has had to, and neither shoots well enough to thrive without it.
flaws.t: Two alpha guards, one ball, and neither is efficient

flaws.b: The top assist man is Pettiford at 3.8, then Kimble at 3.2 — nobody on the roster averaged even 4 assists. For a team this deep in scorers, there's no natural table-setter to organize the touches, which makes the usage overlap harder to solve.
flaws.t: No true distributor and thin guard playmaking

flaws.b: Ngoy is the starting center on an 85 grade and pure projection — zero college minutes. If the freshman isn't SEC-ready, the rim protection plan runs through Oboye and Freeman off the bench, and the starting-five spacing math gets worse when a non-shooting five (Oboye, 24.2% from three) is on the floor.
flaws.t: Interior defense leans on an unproven freshman

positives.b: Dowd (6-8, 1.3 blk, 10.1 rpg) starts next to freshman Ngoy (6-10, 85 grade), and that's before the bench sends 7-1 Oboye (1.2 blk, 66.7 FG%) and Creighton's Freeman (6-10, 0.8 blk, 60.2 FG%). You do not get downhill on this team easily.
positives.t: Rare rim-protection depth for a starting group

positives.b: 41.3% from three on real wing minutes, 44.6% overall, 86% FT, and just 1.0 turnover a game against a 1.3 assist rate. He needs zero touches to help — he spaces, defends (1.1 stl), and never coughs it up. Every ball-dominant lineup needs an Overton, and he's the cleanest fit in the starting five.
positives.t: Kevin Overton is the perfect low-usage 3-and-D wing

positives.b: 14.4/10.1/2.1 with 1.3 blocks at Troy — a double-double machine who blocks shots, passes (2.1 apg is strong for a big), and only turns it over 1.4 times. He rebounds so the small guards don't have to and gives Pearl a stretch look (33.3% from three) at the 4.
positives.t: Thomas Dowd is a genuine two-way anchor at the 4

positives.b: Kimble (18.0 ppg, 2.6 steals) was the alpha at EKU and is a genuine ball-hawk; Pettiford (15.4/3.8, 82.5% FT) is the returning face of the program. There's no shortage of shot-making pressure or downhill juice in the backcourt.
positives.t: Two double-figure lead guards with bite

bench.helps: Unusual quality this deep. Pickens (77, 9.8 ppg, 2.1 apg, 39.2% from three in 27 starter-level minutes at UC Riverside) is a real secondary creator to survive Wright's rest. Baker is a sniper (47.4% 3P, 88.9% FT), Betsey adds another 40.7% shooter, and Mboup is a genuine rebounder (5.1 rpg in just 15.6 minutes). With Pickens at 77 and Baker at 75, there's no cliff off the starting group.
bench.hurts: It doesn't fix the two real holes and it adds one. Mboup can't shoot at all (16.7% 3P, 23.1% FT) — he shrinks the floor and is an outright hack-a-liability late — and he's still not a rim protector at 0.5 blocks. Behind him it's bodies: 6-11 Stewart (66) has literally one minute of TCU tape, and Kozlowski (65) is a mop-up piece. The one player tall enough to protect the rim has never played.

coach.might: Roll out the authored five — Wright/Chandler/Branch/Whalin/Urbaniak — run heavy Wright pick-and-roll with shooters spaced to the corners, lean on Branch's raw talent to be the second scorer, and stagger Pickens in to steady the second unit.
should: Turn it into a track meet. With five 39% shooters and zero rim protection, do not try to win 62-60 grind games in the Big 12 halfcourt — push tempo, hunt early threes, and let your shooting depth decide games your interior defense can't.

Build Chandler into a secondary handler now, so the non-Wright minutes aren't naked. His 2.3 apg / 1.1 TOV profile can bridge Wright's rest better than dumping it all on Pickens, and it gives you a second initiator when defenses load up on Wright.

Solve rim defense with scheme, not personnel. You can't drop-cover with 0.3-block bigs — pre-rotate, wall up the paint, stay foul-conscious, and reserve Mboup's rebounding-and-0.5-block minutes specifically for bruising post teams even though he kills your spacing.
Never close with Mboup. His 23.1% FT is a late-game hack magnet — use him for early rebounding stretches, then go small-and-shooty to finish so opponents can't foul you out of the offense.

Bring Branch along off the ball first. Don't hand an unproven freshman on-ball creation duties — feed him catch-and-shoot looks and cuts off Wright's gravity, and only widen his role once the shot-making proves real.

BYU.essence: BYU is Robert Wright plus a shooting-soaked portal-and-freshman remix. Kevin Young returns one bona-fide alpha — an 87-grade lead guard putting up 18.1/4.6/3.5 on 41% from three — and surrounds him with a rotation stuffed with shooting (five 39%+ shooters across the two units) and two prized, unproven bigs, freshman Bruce Branch (88, the roster's top grade) and international import Jakub Urbaniak (79), who together own zero college minutes. The spacing is genuinely elite and the depth is legitimate. The problems are structural: no true center, no rim protection anywhere on the floor, and a halfcourt offense that lives and dies with one guard.

second_unit.strength: Shot-making and creation hold up. Pickens can run the offense (2.1 apg, 1.5 TOV) while Baker (47.4%) and Betsey (40.7%) space around him and Mboup crashes the glass — the bench can score in bunches without Wright on the floor.
second_unit.weakness: The moment Wright sits, the creation drops off and there is still nobody at the rim; pairing a non-shooting Mboup (23.1% FT) with the reserves either clogs the paint or leaves the interior naked. The unit can outscore you but can't stop anything inside.

flaws.b: The starting five tops out at 6-10 Whalin, who blocked 0.3 per game. Wright (0.0), Chandler (0.3) and Whalin (0.3) mean nobody guards the basket. In the Big 12, where you see a real center most nights, that is a survival-level problem.
flaws.t: No rim protection, no true center

flaws.b: His 4.6 apg is the only real engine; the next-best proven creator is Chandler at 2.3. Ball-handling, shot creation and offensive organization all live in one 6-1 body. There is no second lead guard.
flaws.t: One Wright injury from collapse

flaws.b: Branch (88) and Urbaniak (79) carry the roster's top frontcourt grades entirely on projection. The floor of this starting group is a guess, and it's a guess in the frontcourt where the defense already can't cover.
flaws.t: Two of five starters have zero college sample

flaws.b: 34% from three, 40.3% FG, 5.3 ppg in 20 minutes. He's below the sag-off line, so he's not really a floor-spacer — and at 0.3 blocks he's not a rim protector either. A tweener without a defining skill.
flaws.t: Whalin is the stretch four who doesn't stretch

positives.b: Wright is the stable core almost no rebuild has — 18.1/4.6/3.5 on 41% from deep, 46.7% FG, 82.1% FT and just 2.2 TOV. He scores, distributes, and spaces all at elite clips. Nearly everything good starts with him.
positives.t: A returning alpha who does everything

positives.b: Wright (41%) and Chandler (41%) start it, and Baker (47.4%), Pickens (39.2%) and Betsey (40.7%) extend it off the bench. Five legit 39%+ shooters — you cannot help off this team, which pries open driving lanes for Wright.
positives.t: Genuinely elite spacing, front to back

positives.b: The Kentucky transfer needs no usage: 9.7 ppg on 41% from three, 83.3% FT, 1.1 TOV, plus 1.2 steals. A low-maintenance wing who spaces and defends around the ball-dominant guard — exactly the fit Wright needs.
positives.t: Chandler is plug-and-play 3-and-D

positives.b: Starter grades cluster 78-88 with no obvious hole — even the fourth and fifth options (Whalin 78, Urbaniak 79) grade as functional pieces, not liabilities to hide.
positives.t: No weak statistical link in the five

bench.helps: The second unit is where the quality actually hides. Christian Hammond (82) and Robert Jurkovic (81) both outgrade four of the five starters — Hammond is a 15.6-ppg, 39.3% combo guard and a 1.2-steal on-ball defender, and Jurkovic is a 6-9 international with a top-of-roster grade. Darius Adams (6-5, Maryland pedigree) adds size and portal upside, and Comeh Emuobor and RJ Keene bring 6-5/6-7 rebounding wings (Keene grabbed 4.6 boards in just 22 minutes). This is a rotation eight or nine deep with real ACC bodies.
bench.hurts: The shooting cliff behind McNeil and Yalaho is steep and ugly. Adams shot 24.8% on 3s AND 35.4% overall; Emuobor is an unplayable 10.7% from deep on a 65% free-throw stroke; Keene is a 38% shooter who scored 2.6 a game. Bringing in Adams or Emuobor with Lubin/Evans on the floor gives you a lineup defenses simply won't guard past the arc. And the true bench — Whitty (69), Hall (65), Brim (61) — is developmental filler.

coach.might: Gainey rolls out the authored starting five — Edmead/McNeil/Yalaho/Lubin/Evans — leans on Evans as the defensive anchor and rim-runner, lets Edmead run the offense, and brings Hammond and Jurkovic as his first two off the bench for scoring and size.
should: Fix the frontcourt spacing before anything else: pair Evans with Yalaho (39.8%) as your primary front line, not Lubin. Starting Lubin (27.3%) and Evans (20%) together hands the defense the paint — Yalaho at the 4 pulls a big to the arc and unlocks Evans' rolls and Edmead's drives.

Stop starting your second-best player: Hammond (82) grades above four starters and gives you a 15.6-ppg on-ball defender (1.2 stl). Either start him next to Edmead and split initiation, or explicitly stagger them so one alpha guard anchors every minute — never sit both scoring and playmaking at once.

Resolve the usage collision by role, not hope: make Edmead the primary creator (his 4.4 apg is your only real playmaking) and cast Hammond/McNeil as off-ball scorers running off Evans/Lubin screens. Two alphas guessing whose turn it is will stall in ACC halfcourt sets.

Guard the bench spacing hard: never share the floor with two of {Lubin, Evans, Adams (24.8%), Emuobor (10.7%)} plus a non-shooter — keep at least one of McNeil/Yalaho/Hammond in every five so defenses can't wall off the paint.

Weaponize the size defensively: with Evans (3.3 blk) behind them, let Edmead and Hammond pressure full-court and funnel drives to the rim — turn a middling-shooting roster into a turnovers-and-transition team that scores before defenses set.

NC-State.essence: A physical, top-down rebuild bolted onto two returners (McNeil, Lubin) with roughly a dozen new faces — but unlike a guard-heavy portal job, NC State is built inside-out around a genuinely elite defensive anchor. Kyle Evans (86, 3.3 blocks, 8.7 boards) is the best player and the identity: a rim-protecting, glass-eating center flanked by real interior size in Lubin and Jurkovic. The perimeter is competent and connected — McNeil (42.7%) and Yalaho (39.8%) space it, Edmead and Hammond create it — but the roster's fault lines are classic: two former alpha lead guards sharing one ball, a starting frontcourt (Lubin, Evans) that can't shoot, and a bench headlined by players (Hammond 82) who are frankly better than the starters listed ahead of them. This is a defense-and-rebounding team whose ceiling depends on Gainey solving a spacing-and-usage puzzle in the halfcourt.

second_unit.strength: You can bring a better scorer (Hammond, 15.6) and arguably a better big (Jurkovic, 81) off the bench than you started, so there's no drop-off when the starters rest — a rare luxury. A Hammond-led second unit can attack, defend on the ball, and hold or extend leads.
second_unit.weakness: Assembling a second unit that both spaces and defends is nearly impossible: the non-Hammond bench scorers (Adams, Emuobor, Keene) are all sub-35% shooters, so any group without McNeil or Yalaho on the floor becomes a crowded, non-spaced halfcourt that lets defenses load up on Evans.

flaws.b: Edmead was THE guy at Hofstra; Hammond was THE guy at Santa Clara — and Hammond (grade 82) is buried at the 6-spot behind him. Both need touches to score; neither is a natural 2.5-assist connector. Someone has to accept a secondary role they've never played, or the offense stagnates into hero-ball.
flaws.t: Two alpha guards, one ball

flaws.b: Lubin (27.3% on 3s) and Evans (20%) are non-spacers who live at the rim. Start them together and defenses sag the lane, wall off Evans, and dare NC State to beat them from outside — squeezing the very driving room McNeil's and Edmead's games need.
flaws.t: The starting frontcourt can't shoot

flaws.b: Edmead's 4.4 apg is the only meaningful table-setting on the roster; Hammond (2.5), McNeil (0.8), Yalaho (1.7) don't create for others. If Edmead sits or is pressured off the ball, ball movement dries up fast.
flaws.t: One real playmaker, and he's a scorer first

flaws.b: Only McNeil and Lubin return; the other three starters (Edmead/Hofstra, Yalaho/Wazzu, Evans/UC Irvine) are brand-new, and two are stepping up multiple levels of competition. Expect early-season chemistry lags on defensive rotations and half-court reads.
flaws.t: A portal roster with almost no continuity

positives.b: Kyle Evans is the roster's best player and its defensive spine: 3.3 blocks, 8.7 rebounds, 62% inside. He erases drives and lets the perimeter defenders pressure up top. No other player on the board grades within four points of him.
positives.t: An elite, grade-86 rim anchor

positives.b: Paul McNeil (42.7% on 3s, 82.4% FT, 6-5) is a plug-and-play movement shooter, and stretch-four Eemeli Yalaho (39.8%) lets you pull a big to the arc. You cannot help off McNeil, and Yalaho's shooting keeps the lane from collapsing on Evans.
positives.t: The wing shooting is real

positives.b: Edmead (16.1 ppg, 4.4 apg, 38.7% at Hofstra) and Hammond (15.6, 39.3% at Santa Clara) both put up double-digit scoring as primary options. You are not short on players who can get their own bucket in an ACC halfcourt.
positives.t: Two proven shot-creators in the backcourt

positives.b: Evans (8.7) and Lubin (7.1, 66.8% FG, 0.9 blk) give you two 6-9/6-10 bodies who rebound and finish. Add Jurkovic (6-9) off the bench and this is a big, physical frontcourt few ACC opponents will out-muscle.
positives.t: Legitimate size and glass control

bench.helps: The headline is Damon Wilkinson — an 81-grade, 13.9-and-6.4 center on 58.9% shooting coming off the bench. That's a starter almost anywhere, and it means the drop from Kapke to the backup 5 is essentially zero. Cale Jacobsen (36.6% from three on 52.1% FG) is a legitimate connective shooter, and Degourville (3.0 apg) gives you a nominal backup ballhandler.
bench.hurts: Behind Wilkinson and Jacobsen the floor caves in. Connor Essegian collapsed to 25.8% from three on 31.8% FG — an R-Sr. you can't leave on the floor. Degourville can pass but can't score (5.5 ppg on 37.1% FG). The rest is unproven: freshmen Rice and Lanier, a 70-grade Cooper and 67-grade Betts with no real sample, and Curtis (71) is a 7-1 project at 3.6 career mpg. Grades slide from 81/82 in the top group to 69–65 at the back — the quality cliff is steep and it comes fast.

coach.might: Play fast and five-out — let Sandfort fly off screens, put the ball in Leonhardt's hands in pick-and-roll, surround them with three shooters, and bomb threes at a high volume. Classic Hoiberg offense-first tempo, leaning on the elite spacing and hoping the scoring outruns the defensive leaks.
should: Stagger the two 81-grade centers — never share the floor. Kapke and Wilkinson both block under one shot per game, so a two-big lineup only compounds the rim-protection problem while clogging your spacing. Bridge their minutes instead so one always-scoring, always-rebounding big anchors every unit for a full 40.

Weaponize the spacing by playing Orme (39.7%) at the 5 in small-ball stretches. Dragging Kapke's or Wilkinson's man to the arc opens the entire lane for Leonhardt's drives and gives Sandfort room to attack closeouts — this is the lineup that turns 'good shooting' into 'unguardable.'

Defend the paint by scheme, not by blocks. With no eraser, wall up and force baseline drives into help rather than gambling for swats. Give the 7-1 Curtis a defined change-of-pace role purely as a rim deterrent against downhill teams, even if he can't do much else yet.

Cut Essegian's minutes and hand them to Jacobsen. A 25.8%/31.8% shooter drowns your best asset (spacing); Jacobsen's 36.6%/52.1% keeps the floor honest when the starters rest. Don't let loyalty to the R-Sr. sink the second unit's geometry.

Protect Leonhardt and script for his absence. He's the only creator, at 34.4 mpg — build set actions (Sandfort DHOs, Orme high-post touches) that manufacture offense when he sits, and keep a shooter next to Degourville at all times so the non-scoring backup PG can still function as a connector, not a scorer.

Nebraska.essence: A portal build with a real spine — eight new faces layered onto two returning wings, but unlike a blank-slate overhaul this one is anchored by its best player. Pryce Sandfort (82, 18.1 ppg, 41.6% from three) is a returning, movement-shooting alpha, and Braden Frager (79) came back with him. Around them Hoiberg imported a pass-first lead guard (Leonhardt), a stretch four (Orme, 39.7%), and two 81-grade centers (Kapke, Wilkinson). The identity is clean: elite, four-out spacing, defined roles with no ball-dominance collision, and rare starter-quality depth at the 5. The catch is the part every Hoiberg roster tends to skimp on — nobody protects the rim, and there's no proven second creator if Leonhardt sits.

second_unit.strength: Wilkinson is the whole reason the second unit functions — a genuine double-double center who's better than most leagues' starters. Run him with Jacobsen's shooting and Degourville's passing and the bench can hold a lead without the offense drying up, because the big keeps producing and the spacing survives.
second_unit.weakness: The bench backcourt cannot generate its own shot. Degourville (37.1% FG) is a distributor who can't finish, Jacobsen is a catch-and-shoot piece, and Essegian's stroke abandoned him (25.8%/31.8%). When a second-unit possession breaks down and the clock hits five, nobody on the floor can create a bucket off the dribble — everything has to come from Wilkinson or a Leonhardt/Sandfort stagger.

flaws.b: Kapke blocks 0.4 and Orme 0.7 — the starting frontcourt deters nothing at the basket, and 6-11 Kapke is a positional big, not a shot-eraser. The only 7-footer, Curtis, has 3.6 career mpg. For an offense-first Hoiberg team, this is the fault line opponents will attack downhill all night.
flaws.t: No rim protection, full stop

flaws.b: Orme hits 63.6% from the line and Kapke 70.7% — with backup Wilkinson at 72%, every late-game possession that funnels to the frontcourt is a hack-a liability. In a two-possession B10 game, that's points you're gifting back.
flaws.t: The bigs can't shoot free throws

flaws.b: Leonhardt's 6.0 apg carries the offense; the next-best returning distributor in the top five is Sandfort at 2.0. If Leonhardt is pressured, in foul trouble, or resting his 34.4 mpg, there is no one else who bends a defense off the dribble.
flaws.t: One creator, no plan B

flaws.b: The 39.7% from three is real spacing, but at 6-9 he's a 12.7-and-5 four who blocks 0.7 and shoots 63.6% FT — a floor-spacer, not a stopper or a physical rebounder. Pair him with the non-blocking Kapke and the interior gets soft in a hurry.
flaws.t: Orme's efficiency profile is thin

positives.b: Four starters shoot it: Sandfort 41.6%, Orme 39.7%, Leonhardt 36.8%, Frager 35.2% — two comfortably above 39. You cannot pack the paint against this group. It opens driving lanes for Leonhardt and clean roll windows for Kapke.
positives.t: Genuinely elite, verified spacing

positives.b: Sandfort is unambiguously THE scorer (18.1 on 0.7 turnovers), and Leonhardt is the distributor (6.0 apg) who scores inside the offense (11.9 on 50.5% FG). Nobody else needs the ball to be effective. This is the opposite of a two-alpha-guard tug-of-war — the pecking order writes itself.
positives.t: Clean role definition, no usage collision

positives.b: Leonhardt pulls 5.4 rpg from the point, and four starters sit at 4.9+ (Kapke 5.7, Orme 5.0, Sandfort 4.9). No single dominant glass-eater, but they gang-rebound and the point guard finishing plays on the defensive glass fuels the break Hoiberg wants.
positives.t: Guard-driven rebounding by committee

positives.b: Sandfort (the leading scorer AND highest grade at 82) and Frager both return as R-So. wings. The best player already knows the system — this rebuild has continuity where it matters most, not a locker room of ten strangers.
positives.t: A returner anchor amid the portal churn

bench.helps: Braeden Smith (Gonzaga) is the one true point guard on the roster — 3.6 apg to 1.1 TO in just 17 mpg, an 80.5% FT stroke, and a 1.0 steal rate. He is a better distributor than anyone in the starting five and quietly stabilizes the second unit. Devin Brown (Davidson, 79 grade) has starter-caliber upside, and Ahneman (76, 6-11) gives real size behind Duncomb.
bench.hurts: The shooting falls off a cliff behind the top two wings. Brown hit 31% from three and 63% from the line; Imes 32.5% from three on a brutal 52.4% FT; Smith 33.3%; Dortch and Diallo are non-shooters. A bench built to preserve leads instead clogs the floor and can't make free throws — Imes and Dortch (53.6%) are late-game liabilities.

coach.might: Roll it out the obvious way: freshman Sanderson at the point running Shrewsberry's motion offense, Braeden Shrewsberry and Ethan Roberts spacing the wings, Koehler at the four as a stretch big, and Duncomb as the featured post hub — pound it inside to the 18-and-9 center and let the shooters spot up around him.
should: Discount the counting stats on your two alphas. Duncomb's 18/9 came against Big South bodies and Roberts' 16.9 against the Ivy League — neither has been the go-to guy in the ACC. Build the halfcourt around Duncomb's proven efficiency (60% FG) as a screener and post scorer, but let Roberts' 40% catch-and-shoot stroke, not his off-the-dribble reps, be his ACC role until he proves he can create at this level.

Solve the point guard problem honestly. You are starting a freshman (Sanderson, no sample) at the one while your only real distributor — Smith, 3.6 apg to 1.1 TO — sits. Close games with Smith on the floor next to Sanderson; you cannot survive ACC ball pressure with a rookie as your sole primary handler.

Protect your spacing at all costs. You have exactly two plus shooters in Roberts (40.4%) and Shrewsberry (40.2%), plus Koehler at 38.2%. Never play Smith, Imes, and a non-shooting big together — that lineup gives help defenders permission to wall off Duncomb. Keep at least two of your three real shooters on the floor every second.

Manufacture rim protection you don't have. Nobody blocks shots — Duncomb and Koehler each at 0.7-0.8, and the 7-1 freshman Solongo (69 grade) is raw. Duncomb is a below-the-rim anchor, so defend in a scheme that keeps him near the basket: drop coverage, wall-ups, and gang rebounding, because outside of Duncomb's 8.9 boards this team has no proven rebounder.

Notre Dame.essence: A returner-anchored core (Braeden Shrewsberry, Koehler, Imes) wrapped in a targeted portal haul, built around two double-digit scorers who dominated smaller conferences — Duncomb (18/9 from Winthrop) and Roberts (16.9 from Penn). The offense flows through a bruising 60%-shooting center with two genuine 40% wing shooters around him. But the spacing is thin past those two, the point guard spot is a freshman leap of faith, and the whole team blocks almost nothing — an ACC roster with a clear identity inside and real, nameable holes on the perimeter and at the rim.

second_unit.strength: Genuine size and a real floor general. Smith (3.6 apg, 1.0 stl) can actually run a unit, and 6-11 Ahneman plus 6-9 Dortch (61% FG, 0.7 blk) give the second group more length than most benches — Dortch is an efficient rim-runner in a small role.
second_unit.weakness: It cannot shoot or make free throws. Once Roberts and Shrewsberry sit, the floor shrinks — Brown (31%), Imes (32.5%), and Smith (33.3%) are all below-average from deep, and the unit's collective free-throw shooting (Imes 52.4%, Dortch 53.6%) turns close bench minutes into a giveaway.

flaws.b: Jonathan Sanderson (Fr., no college sample) is penciled in as the starting one while the roster's only true distributor — Smith, 3.6 apg — comes off the bench. That's an enormous bet on an unproven rookie to handle ACC pressure and feed the offense.
flaws.t: A freshman is the entire point guard plan

flaws.b: Duncomb's 18/9 was against the Big South and Roberts' 16.9 against the Ivy League. Neither has scored a bucket in a high-major game. Expecting those exact numbers to survive ACC size and length is the roster's biggest projection risk.
flaws.t: Both alphas are level-jumping

flaws.b: For a lineup with two 6-10 bigs, the shot-blocking is alarming — Duncomb 0.8, Koehler 0.7 per game. This is a below-the-rim front line that will have to scheme its interior defense rather than erase mistakes at the basket.
flaws.t: Nobody protects the rim

flaws.b: Strip out Duncomb's 8.9 and the starting five is thin on the glass — Roberts (3.9), Koehler (3.2), Shrewsberry (3.1). If Duncomb sits or gets into foul trouble, there is no proven second rebounder to hold the defensive glass.
flaws.t: Rebounding rests on one man

positives.b: Logan Duncomb (83 grade, the roster's best player) put up 18.3 and 8.9 on 60% shooting at Winthrop. He's a genuine post scorer and by far the team's best rebounder — the offense has a real go-to identity inside, and 60% FG means the touches aren't wasted.
positives.t: A proven, efficient interior hub

positives.b: Roberts (40.4% on volume) and returner Braeden Shrewsberry (40.2%, 77.8% FT) give the starting group real, chartable spacing on the wings. Defenses cannot sag off both to load up on Duncomb, which is exactly the geometry a post-up offense needs.
positives.t: Two legitimate 40% wing shooters

positives.b: Brady Koehler (6-10) shot 38.2% from three and 45.2% overall in a bench role last year. A big who spaces to the corner lets Duncomb operate without a second non-shooter clogging the paint — the one starter whose skill set is tailor-made for this lineup.
positives.t: A stretch four who fits

positives.b: Braeden Shrewsberry returns as a senior who already knows his father's offense inside out — 11.9 ppg, 40% from three, only 1.1 turnovers a night. Real shot-making plus zero learning curve is valuable glue on a heavily-rebuilt roster.
positives.t: Coach's-son continuity in the system
